title: Consecration to Mary
hook: John Paul II's motto was totally yours, from Montfort

segments.voice: Yesterday, La Vang: Catholics hiding in a Vietnamese forest, told to boil the leaves for healing. Your line was in the forest. What help did you find already within reach? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

Bishops' coats of arms can get crowded: keys, lions, towers, a shell or two. When Karol Wojtyła became a bishop in Poland, his was nearly empty. A plain cross, a little off center. Beneath one arm of it, a capital M, for Mary, standing near the cross the way she stood near it on Calvary. And under the shield, two Latin words. He kept them when he became Pope John Paul the Second, under the same plain cross. Today's word is those two words.
screen: `A NEARLY EMPTY COAT OF ARMS.` → `A CROSS, AND AN M BENEATH IT.` → `TWO LATIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Totus tuus: totally yours. They're spoken to Mary, but they're not about her alone. Second, where he found them. A French priest, Louis de Montfort, wrote a book on what he called true devotion to Mary. Its center is an act Catholics call consecration: giving yourself entirely to Jesus, through Mary. Your prayers, your work, your days, all handed to her, so she can bring them to her son. Totus tuus comes out of that tradition. Third, a young man's worry. John Paul wrote that as a young man he had worried that loving Mary too much might crowd out Christ. Reading Montfort changed his mind. He came to see that devotion to Mary, done rightly, doesn't stop at her. It leads to Christ, the way a mother takes your hand and walks you to her son. Fourth, where it ends. Paul, writing to the Galatians, describes a life handed over so completely that it is no longer only his own. In the Douay-Rheims: "And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me." Consecration, in this tradition, aims there: Mary is the way in, and her son is the one it reaches. This week we went to the places where Catholics remember her coming: a spring at Lourdes, children at Fatima, a silent wall at Knock, schoolgirls at Kibeho, a shore at Vailankanni, a forest at La Vang. Today we stay home, with two words a pope wore under a cross.
screen: `TOTALLY YOURS.` · `MONTFORT: TO JESUS, THROUGH MARY.` · `A WORRY ANSWERED.` · `NOW NOT I, BUT CHRIST.` · then, large: `CHRIST LIVETH IN ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer Mary one day. Settle, and breathe. Walk through today in your mind, or tomorrow if today is nearly done: the first thing you'll do, the people you'll see, the job you're dreading, the meal, the tired end of it. Don't fix any of it. Just look at it whole. Then, in your imagination, hand the whole day over, the way you'd hand a child to someone you trust. If you pray, you can say a Hail Mary and the two words of the motto: totus tuus. If you don't, simply hold the day loosely, as something given. The bell holds the time.
Totus Tuus. Latin for totally yours: John Paul the Second's motto, taken from Montfort's consecration of oneself to Jesus through Mary. Today's word, and the end of this week.
Your line: totally yours. Today, give one person or one task your whole attention, no phone, no half-listening, for as long as it takes. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: Some Catholics make a consecration to Jesus through Mary, often following Louis de Montfort's method of preparation, and some renew it each year; Pope John Paul II took Totus Tuus, from this tradition, as his motto.

fork.setup: you're a young man who loves Christ, and you worry that devotion to Mary might crowd him out. what do you do?
options: drop Marian devotion to be safe.
read Montfort, and give yourself to Jesus through Mary.
keep Mary and Jesus in separate corners of your prayer.
fork.reveal: John Paul II wrote that he had that worry, and that Montfort answered it: devotion to Mary, done rightly, leads to Christ. he took totus tuus as his motto.

original.note: Latin: totally yours. both words agree with the one speaking, a man; a woman would say tota tua.

trapdoor: what you thought: a pope's slogan.
what it means: a consecration: giving yourself wholly to Jesus through Mary, until, in Paul's words, Christ lives in you.
what a scholar hears: Louis de Montfort's true devotion, read by a young Karol Wojtyła, with Galatians 2:20 as its goal.

Coat of arms description (a plain cross set off center, a capital M below its right arm, motto Totus Tuus): confirm. 'Bishops' coats of arms can get crowded' is a light general remark; confirm or cut.
That John Paul II kept the coat of arms and motto as pope: confirm.

John Paul II's account of worrying that devotion to Mary might crowd out Christ, and Montfort resolving it, is paraphrased from Gift and Mystery (and Crossing the Threshold of Hope); not quoted (copyrighted). Confirm.

The fuller formula 'Totus tuus ego sum, et omnia mea tua sunt' is associated with Montfort (who draws it from earlier sources); the script says only that totus tuus 'comes out of that tradition'. Confirm.
Montfort's consecration described as 'giving yourself entirely to Jesus, through Mary'; howItsDone mentions a period of preparation and yearly renewal; confirm.
